Microbial community dynamics and volatile fatty acid production during 
anaerobic digestion of microaerated food waste under different 
organic loadings
Farrukh Raza Amin a,b,c,1, Habiba Khalid a,b,d,1, Jingjing Wang a,b, Yaxiang Li a,b, Longxue Ma a,b,  
Wuxi Chen a,b, Yu Duan a,b, Yida Zhai a,b, Demao Li a,b,*
a Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tianjin 300308, China
b National Innovation Centre for Synthetic Biology, Tianjin 300308, China
c Department of Chemistry, COMSATS University Islamabad, Park Road, Tarlai Kalan 45550, Islamabad, Pakistan
d Department of Applied Bioeconomy, Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, 50-375 Wrocław, Poland

Keywords:
Food waste
Oxygen pretreatment
Organic loading
Volatile fatty acids
Microbial community analysis
A B S T R A C T
This study examined the effects of microaeration pretreatment and varying organic loading rates (OLRs) on 
volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production from food waste (FW) via anaerobic digestion process. FW was pretreated 
with 6 mL O2/g VS and digested at OLRs ranging from 10 to 25 g/L VS. Microaeration pretreatment increased the 
VFA yield to 7.4 g/L, whereas without pretreatment, it was 5.19 g/L, with butyrate as the dominant VFA (92 % at 
25 g/L OLR) due to Firmicutes enrichment. A relatively high OLR initially increased VFA production but later 
favored propionate without pretreatment. Microbial analysis revealed that aerobic conditions promoted lactic 
acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus, increasing lactic acid production, whereas anaerobic conditions promoted 
Prevotella and butyrate producers such as Clostridium, which specialize in acetate and butyrate production. This 
study highlights that microaeration and an optimal OLR can increase and stabilize VFA yields, modulating the 
microbial community for tailored VFA profiles that are useful in biofuel and biochemical applications.
1. Introduction
The midterm reorientation of waste management is anticipated to be 
due to the current change in waste policy within the circular economy. A 
significant improvement over the previous regulations is the inclusion of 
specific measures to manage waste and encourage the reuse of materials. 
Moreover, the perception of waste has shifted from being an undesirable 
product that can be costly to handle and dispose of (Aguirre-Garcia, 
2019).
Food waste (FW) is produced in factories and kitchens and consists of 
both leftover cooked food and raw ingredients. FW is the main compo­
nent of municipal solid waste (MSW), which accounts for 37–62 % of 
MSW in China and 12–30 % of MSW in certain developed countries, such 
as the USA, Singapore, and England (Wang et al., 2020). Although 870 
million people are chronically undernourished, 1.3 billion to 1.6 billion 
tons of food waste constitute a quarter of global food production 
(Braguglia et al., 2018). The level of social and economic development 
in an area has a significant effect on the quantity of FW. Europe and 
North America have FW yields per capita of approximately 0.26–0.32 
kg/d, whereas Africa and Southeast Asia have yields of only 0.02–0.053 
kg/d (Bao et al., 2015). By 2025, Asia is expected to experience an in­
crease in FW from 2.78 billion tons to 4.16 billion tons. The annual 
growth rate of FW has surpassed 10 % in recent years, especially in 
China, as a result of the acceleration of industrial development and

The expanding worldwide population has led to a surge in the 
number of FW in need of adequate pretreatment. Compared with other 
pretreatment methods, such as landfilling, incineration, and compost­
ing, FW acidogenic fermentation for VFAs has gained widespread 
acceptance as a versatile and environmentally friendly method. On the 
other hand, short-chain carboxylic acids (SCCA), such as acetic acid, 
propionic acid, and butyric acid, are valuable platform chemicals 
generated during acidogenic processes (Bhatt et al., 2020). With a price 
range of 2000–2500 USD/t, butyric acid is considered an important 
chemical product among SCCAs and is significantly more expensive than 
acetic acid is (400–900 USD/t) (Bastidas-Oyanedel and Schmidt, 2019). 
Moreover, butyric acid can be used in a variety of ways as an interme­
diary or feedstock in the food, pharmaceutical, and chemical industries 
and thus has considerable commercial potential (Jiang et al., 2018). This 
process not only stabilizes these wastes but also offers an opportunity for 
chemical and energy recovery (Wainaina et al., 2019). The widely 
implemented process of anaerobic digestion (AD) is used to obtain 
value-added chemicals and methane from FW (Tenci et al., 2023). Mi­
crobial communities naturally decompose organic matter into methane- 
rich biogas through different stages, which can then be used for heating, 
electricity, or fuel. Research has focused mostly on the use of anaerobic 
digestion to produce useful byproducts other than methane, such as H2 
and carboxylic acids, including lactic acid, succinic acid, and VFAs 
(Kleerebezem et al., 2015; Selder et al., 2021; Uddin and Wright, 2023).
The enzymatic hydrolysis of FW needs to be improved to produce 
more VFAs. Pretreating FW via physical, chemical, and biological pre­
treatments is a common practice. Physical procedures are used to 
decrease the substrate’s particle size, whereas chemical pretreatment 
makes use of chemicals to increase biomass digestibility. However, these 
pretreatments are energy intensive and need to be handled carefully 
(Amin et al., 2017; Viancelli et al., 2023). The incorporation of 
microaeration pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis enhances the ef­
ficiency of VFAs production. This pretreatment process involves mi­
croorganisms being partially exposed to oxygen under moderate 
operating conditions. This process accelerates the hydrolysis stage by 
encouraging microbial activity and cell growth (Wagner et al., 2018). 
The conversion of FW into valuable VFAs is more efficient with the 
integration of microaeration pretreatment, which reduces the lag phase 
time and increases the maximum VFAs production rate. By adopting this 
holistic approach, we can efficiently utilize FW to generate VFAs for 
various biofuel or chemical production applications (Amin et al., 2021b; 
Ladero et al., 2018). The potential role of oxygen in regulating the or­
ganization of the microbial community makes it difficult to reconcile the 
beneficial and detrimental effects of microaeration during AD. A thor­
ough examination of the underlying processes is also needed to obtain a 
deeper understanding of the microaeration pretreatment procedure.
This study chose a microbial reagent from pig slurry (PS), which is 
known to be essential for hydrolyzing FW and has diverse combinations 
of beneficial microbes from various development conditions, to perform 
microaeration pretreatment. The role of facultative bacteria in microa­
eration pretreatment is significant, as it is a biological process. The 
growth rate of facultative bacteria increases under microaerobic con­
ditions, resulting in the production of fewer extracellular enzymes, such 
as cellulase and protease, which ultimately leads to a more efficient 
hydrolysis process. In Fu, the increase in Firmicutes abundance resulted 
in increased hydrolysis under microaerated conditions (Fu et al., 2016; 
Wang et al., 2024). The primary goals of this research are to (1) create a 
sustainable pretreatment technique that increases the production of 
VFAs in FW; (2) examine the effects of variations in organic loading in 
the fed-batch process of AD on VFAs production; and (3) look into the 
changes that occur in microbial communities throughout the AD process 
and how functional microorganisms react to different oxygen 
concentrations.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Feedstock and inoculum
FW was collected from a canteen located at the Tianjin Institute of 
Industrial Biotechnology, Tianjin, China, and ground (to homogenize) 
with a high-speed grinder (XINGSHILIHE, Beijing, China) prior to being 
added to the fermentation system. PS was collected from farms in 
Hainan Dongzhaigang, China, and used as the startup inoculum for the 
AD process.
2.2. Oxygen pretreatment
One-liter bottles were used for oxygen pretreatment. A total volume 
of 100 mL was formed by mixing 10 g of wet food waste, 20 mL of PS, 
and deionized water during pretreatment. Then, the bottles were flushed 
with N2 for 3 min to exhaust all the air, and the bottles were closed with 
a rubber stopper. After removing all the air from the bottles, 48 mL of 
oxygen was added to each bottle at atmospheric pressure via a syringe to 
achieve an oxygen level of 6 mL/g VS (marked as O2 pretreated). We 
obtained this information from our previous study, where we optimized 
the oxygen load (Amin et al., 2021b). The process of oxygen pretreat­
ment was performed in duplicate, and two bottles were placed without 
oxygen pretreatment as a control (marked without oxygen pretreat­
ment). All the bottles were placed in a water bath at 37 ◦C and mixed 
with a magnetic stirrer during oxygen pretreatment.
2.3. Organic loading
Two identical reactors equipped with mixers were operated in fed- 
batch mode, employing both feeding and draw-off methods. The ex­
periments were initiated under controlled conditions, maintaining a 
constant temperature of 37 ◦C and a neutral pH of 7.0 (set at the start of 
the experiment). The hydraulic retention time (HRT) was adjusted on 
the basis of the depletion of VFAs concentrations, with HRT values set at 
9, 31, and 72 days. The impact of the organuc loading rate (OLR) on the 
process was explored by operating the reactors at OLRs of 10, 15, 20, 
and 25 g/L on a VS basis. The experimental period spanned 125 days, 
aiming to determine the optimal OLR for maximum production of each 
VFA.
2.4. Analytical methods
The FW and PS were analyzed via standard methods to determine the 
total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) (APHA, 2005). The weights of 
the FW and PS were recorded, and the samples were placed in an oven at 
105 ◦C for 24 h to eliminate moisture. To calculate the TS content, as 
shown in Eq. (1), the FW and PS were reweighed after 24 h. The second 
step involved converting the dried samples into ash by heating them in a 
muffle furnace for 2 h at 550 ◦C. The samples were subsequently 
removed from the furnace and cooled to room temperature before being 
weighed again. Eq. (2) shows the calculation of the VS content.

2.5. Anaerobic digestion (AD)
AD was conducted in duplicate. With a feedstock-to-inoculum ratio 
of 1:1, the pretreated FW was inoculated with concentrated PS following 
the complete consumption of oxygen. The working volume was 0.8 mL 
with the use of deionized water. To ensure anaerobic conditions, the 
digesters were refilled with high-purity nitrogen, sealed, and incubated 
in a 37 ◦C water bath for 125 days. The agitation rate for all the digesters 
was maintained at 100 rpm. Samples were collected daily to analyze the 
concentration of VFAs. Fig. 1 shows a schematic illustration of the 
experimental setup.
2.6. Microbial community analysis
Two different stages of digestion were used to extract the genomic 
DNA of bacteria: on the 5th day and on the 97th day. The V3-V4 region of 
the 16S rRNA gene was amplified via the primers 338F (5’-ACTCC­
TACGGGAGGCAGCAGAG-3′) and 806R (5’-GGACTACHGGTGTWTC­
TAAT-3′). The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed with 
initial denaturation at 95 ◦C for 3 min, followed by 25 cycles of 95 ◦C for 
30 s, 55 ◦C for 30 s, and 72 ◦C for 30 s, with a final extension at 72 ◦C for 
5 min. Sequencing was conducted on an Illumina MiSeq platform via 2 
× 300 bp paired-end sequencing chemistry (Majorbio Bio-Pharm 
Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). To produce precisely tailored 
sequences, the sequencing data from MiSeq amplicon sequencing were 
spliced and checked for quality, and the adapters were removed. The 
raw sequences were processed via QIIME2 (version 2020.8). The Ribo­
somal Database Project (RDP) classifier was used to categorize the 
operational taxonomic units (OTUs) by clustering and taxonomically 
classifying them (Wang and Cole, 2024). Diversity analyses were con­
ducted via the phyloseq R package. Dividing the number of sequences by 
the total number of sequences associated with a taxon was used to 
calculate the relative abundance (RA) (Mao et al., 2019). MOTHUR tools 
and Chao1 and ACE estimators were used to calculate the Shannon index 
for species diversity estimation (Li et al., 2018).
2.7. Statistical analysis
All experiments were conducted in duplicate, and the results are 
presented as the mean values. Statistical analyses were performed via 
Origin Pro 9.0 (Origin Lab, USA). To identify significant differences in 
the experimental data, all the data were subjected to analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) and multiple comparisons; a P value of <0.05 was considered 
statistically significant. The diversity indices (Shannon, ACE, and 
Chao1) were calculated via the vegan package in R (version 4.0.3). 
Graphs and figures were generated via Origin Pro 9.0.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characteristics of FW and inoculum
Table 1 outlines the characteristics of the FW and inoculum used in 
the study. The FW contained 21.8 and 19.8 % TS and VS, respectively, 
whereas the inoculum contained only 5.2 % and 2.3 % TS and VS, 
respectively. The FW had a 91.0 % higher VS/TS ratio than did the 
inoculum, suggesting that it has a rich organic composition that is 
conducive to producing VFAs through AD. The pH values of the FW and 
inoculum were initially 4.8 and 8.5, but they were adjusted to 7.1 to 
ensure optimal AD conditions. The results of the nutrient content anal­
ysis revealed that the N2 content in the FW was 3.0 %, which was slightly 
greater than the N2 content in the inoculum, which was 2.7 %. 
Compared with the inoculum, the FW resulted in a significant increase in 
the C content of 47.7 % (26.5 %). The FW had H2 and O2 contents of 
7.45 % and 32.4 %, respectively, whereas the inoculum had H2 contents 
of 3.6 % and O2 contents of 12.2 %. The S content in both the FW and 
inoculum was negligible. The FW and inoculum each had C/N ratios of 
15.9 and 9.8, respectively, which are crucial parameters for AD process. 
This ratio shows that there is a balanced nutrient composition that fa­
cilitates the effective production of VFAs. Owing to its high organic 
content and appropriate nutrient profile, FW is capable of producing 
VFAs through AD, as demonstrated by this detailed analysis.
3.2. Enhancing VFA Production from Food Waste
3.2.1. Impact of the oxygen pretreatment and organic loading rates
By stopping the degradation process at the acidification stage, it is 
possible to modify the conventional AD process to favor the production 
of VFAs instead of methane. To effectively inhibit methanogens, several 
strategies have been explored, including chemical inhibitors, oxygen 
introduction, and substrate loading (Eryildiz and Taherzadeh, 2020). 
This investigation focused on VFAs, which are the primary products of 
the organic matter acidogenesis process, because of their critical role in

presents data on the composition and concentration of VFAs produced 
from FW under different conditions, specifically comparing scenarios 
with and without oxygen pretreatment. The data contained in Table 2
show the VFAs yield at the point of maximum production. Furthermore, 
Fig. 2 shows the dynamic changes in the VFAs concentration and 
composition that occur with and without oxygen pretreatment at 
various OLRs. The concentration of VFAs initially increased in both re­
actors at an OLR of 10 g/L; it peaked on the 5th day in the reactor 
without oxygen pretreatment and on the 8th day in the reactor with 
oxygen pretreatment. On the other hand, after the 7th day, the VFAs 
concentration in the reactor without pretreatment decreased, but the 
VFAs levels in the reactor pretreated with oxygen remained constant. 
This observation led to an increase in the OLR to 15 g/L in both reactors, 
which further increased VFAs production. In the reactor without oxygen 
pretreatment, the highest VFAs generation occurred on day 12, whereas 
in the reactor with oxygen pretreatment, it occurred on day 13. After 
that, only the reactor without oxygen pretreatment presented a decrease 
in the VFAs concentration, which led to an increase in the OLR from 15 
g/L to 20 g/L, leading to possible improvements in VFAs generation. On 
the 33rd day, the reactor with no oxygen pretreatment presented the 
highest VFAs output. On the other hand, the oxygen-treated reactor 
demonstrated steady VFAs generation, with the greatest output recorded 
on the 31st day, whereas a decreasing trend was detected from the 33rd 
to the 70th day. This trend led to a further increase in the OLR to 25 g/L, 
which, on the 92nd day in the reactor without oxygen pretreatment, 
produced the greatest amount of VFAs and was stable until the 125th 
day. In contrast, the highest VFAs production in the oxygen-treated 
reactor was noted on the 96th day, and VFAs production remained sta­
ble throughout the study period. In the fermentation process, the start- 
up phase was characterized by a gradual increase in the OLR to ach­
ieve a balance between alkalinity and acidification. The fermentation 
conducted at 37 ◦C had distinct outcomes on the basis of the oxygen 
availability in the reactors. In reactors without oxygen, butyrate 
emerged as the dominant VFA, constituting 81.3 vol% of all products at 
an OLR of 10 g/L, followed by acetate (9.4 vol%) and propionate (9.2 vol 
%). Notably, ethanol was absent under these conditions. Conversely, in 
the oxygen-treated reactors, the butyrate concentration increased to 
91.5 vol%, whereas the propionate and acetate concentrations 
decreased significantly to 7.1 and 1.0 vol%, respectively. This trend of 
butyrate dominance persisted across higher OLRs (15, 20, and 25 g/L) in 
both the oxygen- and non‑oxygen-treated reactors. Without oxygen 
pretreatment, the percentage of butyrate slightly decreased with 
increasing OLR (74.3, 70.5, and 69.4 vol%, respectively), whereas the 
percentage of propionate increased to 26 vol%. In contrast, the oxygen- 
treated reactors maintained or increased butyrate dominance (91.5, 
85.5, 75.9, and 92.0 vol% across the OLRs tested), as shown in Table 2. 
These findings indicate that oxygen availability significantly (P < 0.05) 
influences VFA production during fermentation, with oxygen pretreat­
ment favoring butyrate production. These findings suggest potential 
strategies for optimizing VFAs production through oxygen management 
in fermentation processes. The observed trends in butyrate production, 
in addition to the increasing concentrations of propionate during 
fermentation, suggest a potential shift in microbial populations favoring 
butyric acid-producing microorganisms, such as Clostridium species. 
This hypothesis aligns with previous findings by Komemoto et al. 
(2009), who reported high butyrate concentrations of 5600–6000 mg/L 
at 37 ◦C (Bhatt et al., 2020; Komemoto et al., 2009). Additionally, the 
study revealed optimal VFAs production at pH values ranging from 6.6 
to 4.4, suggesting that hydrolytic enzyme activities thrive within this pH 
range (Fonseca et al., 2020), further increasing acid production, which is 
similar to the findings of Jiang et al. (Jiang et al., 2013). The variation in 
VFA content due to oxygen pretreatment reflects, to some extent, 
whether this technology could increase hydrolysis to yield more soluble 
small-molecule substances for acid production (Eryildiz and Taherza­
deh, 2020). As shown in Fig. 2, oxygen pretreatment with the inoculum 
agent resulted in greater VFAs production than did pretreatment 
without oxygen. Overall, this approach not only increases the yield and 
stability of VFAs but also shifts the fermentation product spectrum, of­
fering promising avenues for bioenergy and biochemical production 
from organic waste (Wang et al., 2024).
Notably, there were notable alterations in the VFA composition, even 
though the data in Table 2 indicate that the impact of oxygen pre­
treatment on overall VFA generation was rather minor. The distribution 
of individual VFAs was significantly affected by oxygen pretreatment, 
even if the total VFA yields were similar for pretreated and nonpre­
treated samples (e.g., 7.1 g/L for both the OLR 15 and the 7.4 g/L vs. 7.8 
g/L at the OLR 25). For example, compared with the nonpretreated 
sample, the pretreated sample demonstrated a significant increase in 
butyrate production (92.0 vol% vs. 69.4 vol%) and a decrease in pro­
pionate production (3.5 vol% vs. 24.9 vol%) at an OLR of 25. The main 
impact of oxygen pretreatment appears to be this change in the VFAs 
profile rather than the total VFAs yield. The variability of microbial 
communities and the complexity of food waste may be the reasons for 
the comparable total VFA outputs. Pretreatment might have improved 
some metabolic pathways, especially those that support the formation of 
butyrate, but it is also likely that other factors, such as the availability of 
substrate or the rates at which microbes grow, limited the total amount 
of VFAs that could be produced. These results emphasize the importance 
of considering both the composition and total yield of VFAs when 
assessing pretreatment effects. Even if overall yields remain the same, 
the capacity to modify VFAs profiles through oxygen pretreatment may 
be useful for customizing VFAs production for certain downstream uses.
To further evaluate the efficiency of the VFAs production process, we 
calculated the VFAs yield and productivity for each condition. The VFAs 
yield, expressed as (gCOD/L VFA)/(gCOD/L fed), provides insight into 
the conversion efficiency of the substrate to VFAs. The VFAs produc­
tivity, expressed as gCOD/(L × day), indicates the rate of VFAs pro­
duction. The results are presented in Table 3. The VFAs yield decreased 
with increasing OLR for both oxygen pretreated and untreated samples, 
suggesting that higher OLRs may lead to less efficient conversion of the 
substrate to VFAs. The highest yield was observed at the lowest OLR (10

3.3. Ammonia nitrogen and COD analysis at different OLRs
The fluctuations in the NH4
+-N and COD concentrations in the hy­
drolysate with different OLRs with and without oxygen pretreatment are 
illustrated in Fig. 3. Fig. 3 (A) shows the NH4
+-N concentration data 
variability across different phases of the experiment, reflecting how the 
microbial community responds to changes in OLR without oxygen pre­
treatment. The initial phase (days 1–8) with a 10 g/L OLR showed a 
gradual increase in NH4
+-N levels, indicating initial adaptation. 
Increasing the OLR to 15 g/L (days 9–30) and subsequently to 20 g/L 
(days 31–71) resulted in fluctuating NH4
+-N concentrations, suggesting 
that a stressed microbial environment struggled with nitrogen assimi­
lation. The final phase (days 72–125), with a 25 g/L OLR, presented a 
more stable but elevated NH4
+-N concentration (days 90–100), possibly 
indicating a balance between nitrogen release and assimilation. 
Ammonia is generated during anaerobic fermentation when nitrogenous 
compounds, particularly proteins, are degraded biologically and hy­
drolyzed into amino acids, which are then further degraded into 
ammonia (Jiang et al., 2013; Jun et al., 2009). Proteins are more easily 
hydrolyzed under neutral conditions, leading to a higher concentration 
of NH4
+-N. The low amounts may be explained by a number of variables, 
including the possibility that some of the ammonia nitrogen was trans­
formed during digestion into VFAs or other nitrogenous chemicals and 
that a large portion was ingested by the microbial population for 
development and metabolism (Wang et al., 2015). As previously

3.4. Microbial community analysis of food waste
3.4.1. Species diversity and richness
The findings of an investigation of the microbial diversity and rich­
ness in FW digestates, which are shown in Table 4, demonstrate the 
important influence that oxygen pretreatment has on the microbial 
communities that are involved in the biodegradation process. There 
were noticeable differences in the quantity of operational taxonomic 
units (OTUs) as well as the Shannon, ACE, and Chao1 indices between 
the oxygen-treated and nontreated groups. Understanding the 
complexity of microbial ecosystems requires the use of these metrics, 
which include the ACE and Chao1 indices, which estimate microbial 
richness, and the Shannon index, which represents diversity (Zhi et al., 
2019). Compared with their oxygen-treated counterparts, the microbial 
communities were less rich and diverse on days 5 and 97 because of the 
absence of oxygen pretreatment, as evidenced by decreased OTU 
numbers and ACE and Chao1 indices. The ability of the microbial 
community to degrade FW is enhanced by oxygen pretreatment, which 
increases both the richness and diversity of microbes. The enhanced 
indicators (OTU number, ACE, and Chao1 indices) in samples treated 
with oxygen provide additional evidence of the beneficial effects of 
oxygen on microbial communities. These indicators point to a more 
resilient microbial ecosystem with effective hydrolysis and conversion 
processes. This microbial community enrichment and diversity, partic­
ularly in the oxygen-treated samples, highlights the crucial role that 
microbial dynamics play in maximizing waste-to-energy conversion 
processes. The bacterial coverage was 99 %, confirming the compre­
hensive sequencing depth and ensuring that the diversity within the 
samples was accurately captured and represented in the analysis.

3.4.3. Bacterial genera and species
Fig. 5 shows the short-term (day 5) observations, in which without 
oxygen pretreatment, the community was diverse, with Proteiniphilum 
(27.1 %), Petrimonas (14.1 %), and norank_f_Rikenellaceae (9.3 %) being 
predominant. This diversity indicates that a dense anaerobic microbial 
ecosystem is capable of breaking down complex organic materials. The 
oxygen pretreatment led to a slight reduction in Proteiniphilum domi­
nance to 21.5 %, a significant reduction in Petrimonas abundance to 3 %, 
and an increase in the abundance of norank_f_Rikenellaceae to 14.4 %. 
This indicates a shift toward microbes that can either tolerate or thrive 
in the presence of oxygen. Proteiniphilum contributes to the hydrolysis 
and fermentation of proteins and amino acids, although its direct role in 
VFAs production might be limited compared with its role in breaking 
down complex organic matter (He et al., 2017). An increase in the 
abundance of the methane producer norank_f_Rikenellaceae, which is 
commonly found in anaerobic sludge, indicates an increase in methane 
production, which functions as a sort of rival process for the synthesis of 
medium-chain fatty acids. The presence of Petrimonas under anaerobic 
conditions suggests that it plays a role in the initial stages of organic 
matter breakdown, potentially facilitating the production of acetic acid 
in the presence of elemental sulfur (Wang et al., 2021).
Over the long term (day 97), without oxygen pretreatment, Prevotella 
(37.7 %) and Clostridium sensu Stricto_1 (23.2 %) became dominant. The 
emergence of Prevotella plays a crucial role in the breakdown of proteins 
and carbohydrates, leading to the production of acetate and succinate, 
which are important VFAs in the context of FW degradation at low pH 
(Lebuhn et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2021). With oxygen pretreatment, a 
significant increase in Lactobacillus (43.6 %) was observed, indicating a 
shift toward lactic acid fermentation and other acid fermentation. It is 
involved mainly in lactic acid production but can also contribute to 
acetate and propionate production under certain conditions. Under 
aerobic conditions, its predominance indicates a transition toward lactic

substances, potentially leading to the production of acetate and propi­

into acetate, butyrate, molecular H2, and ammonia by Proteiniphilum, 
which follows both acidogenic and acetogenic pathways (Matthies et al., 
2000). Petrimonas belongs to the phylum Bacteroidetes and ferments 
mannose, maltose, galactose, arabinose, and glucose to produce acetate, 
CO2, and H2. It also ferments carbohydrates, proteins, and certain 
organic acids to produce acetate, CO2, and H2 (Huang et al., 2016). 
Fermentimonas_caenicola and uncultured_bacterium_g_DMER64, present 
under both conditions, contribute to the fermentation process and form 
acetic acid, propionic acid, CO2 and traces of isovaleric acid (Hahnke 
et al., 2016). The increase in f_Lachnospiraceae under aerobic conditions 
indicated a shift toward a community that can contribute to the pro­
duction of butyrate. To synthesize butyrate, metabolic intermediates 
that are necessary for the production of ketone bodies as energy sources 
are used (Kim et al., 2022). Norank_f_Rikenellaceae also increased during

breakdown of organic matter, potentially affecting the VFA profile by 
favoring the production of specific acids to increase methane production

anaerobic conditions (Lebuhn et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2021). Clostridium

tridium butyricum are also notable at 13.7 % and 7.8 %, respectively, 
indicating their importance in butyrate production (Fonseca et al., 2020; 
Mermejo et al., 2022). The abundances of Firmicutes NK4A214 and

diverse butyrate and caproate production potentials. The presence of

chain carboxylate production systems (Esquivel-Elizondo et al., 2021). 
On the other hand, with oxygen pretreatment at 97 days (Fig. 6), 
Lactobacillus species became significantly more prevalent, with Lacto­
bacillus at 22.4 %, Lactobacillus mucosae LM1 at 10.2 %, and Lactobacillus 
plantarum at 6.3 %, highlighting a shift toward lactic acid fermentation. 
The increased prevalence of Lactobacillus species underlines a shift to­
ward lactic acid production, which could compete with or complement 
VFAs production depending on the specific application (Boonkumklao 
et al., 2006). Prevotella sp. 152R-1a was still present but was reduced to 
11.9 %, suggesting its reduced dominance during oxygen pretreatment. 
Significant increases were observed in Clostridium sensu stricto 12 and 
Ruminococcaceae bacterium CPB6, which indicated a variety of microbial 
responses to oxygen availability. The prevalence of Prevotella and Clos­
tridium species indicates that they have high potential for producing 
butyrate, acetate, and other short-chain fatty acids, all of which are 
necessary for the effective breakdown of FW (Ma et al., 2020; Xu et al., 
2021). The variety of microbial species, such as Ruminococcaceae_­
Bacterium_CPB6 and Clostridium sensu stricto, indicated a complicated 
network of pathways resulting in the formation of VFAs during oxygen 
pretreatment. The synthesis of caproic acid from lactate is effectively 
facilitated by Ruminococcaceae_Bacterium_CPB6 (Tao et al., 2017). To 
optimize the AD process, a delicate balance of micronutrients is very 
important. Free metal ions, which include micronutrients such as cal­
cium, magnesium, iron, nickel, and cobalt, have an impact on macro­
nutrients. Enzymes need a limited quantity of metals as cofactors, which 
can disrupt the entire AD process. As previously indicated, certain en­
zymes, such as carbon monoxide dehydrogenase, use cobalt, an essential 
micronutrient, to produce methane from acetate. Various methanogenic 
strains contain copper as an adjuvant. Because of its low cost and 
conductive properties, iron is one of the most abundant elements. It can 
activate many enzymes, including pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase, 
and discharge extracellular polymers. For autotrophic methanogenesis 
to occur, nickel is necessary for molecules known as F factor 430 in cells, 
which are found in all methanogenic bacteria. Owing to their impor­
tance for enzymes found in acetoclastic methanogenesis pathways in the 
presence of vitamins, such as carbon monoxide dehydrogenase, acetyl- 
CoA decarboxylase, methyl-H 4 STP: HS-CoM methyltransferase, 
methyl-CoM reductase, and others, nickel, copper, and iron are the most 
frequently studied nutrient supplements in the AD process (Izadi et al., 
2020).
The presence of anaerobic conditions creates a community of mi­
crobes that can ferment complex organics into a wide range of VFAs, 
which are crucial for the efficient degradation of FW. However, aerobic 
conditions seem to promote a different microbial community structure, 
possibly leading to a varied VFAs production profile, with potential 
shifts toward specific VFAs depending on the oxygen levels and micro­
bial interactions. The shifts in microbial dominance and diversity be­
tween the two conditions suggest that environmental management, 
specifically oxygen regulation, could be leveraged to optimize VFAs 
production for bioenergy applications or as precursors in biochemical 
processes.
4. Conclusions and practical implications
This study demonstrates the significant potential of microaeration 
pretreatment in enhancing VFAs production from FW through AD. Key 
findings include the substantial increase in total VFAs yield, with a 
maximum of 7.4 g/L achieved through pretreatment. Microaeration 
altered the microbial community composition, favoring butyrate- 
producing Firmicutes and resulting in butyrate dominance (up to 92 % 
of total VFAs). Research has revealed how environmental factors, 
particularly oxygen availability, shape specialized microbial pop­
ulations for tailored VFAs profiles. By combining microaeration pre­
treatment with organic loading optimization, this study presents a novel 
approach to improve and stabilize VFAs yields.
Some potential future implementations of this study that could be 
explored on the basis of butyric acid pathways are as follows:
1. As the study showed that butyrate production was favored under 
oxygen pretreatment conditions, further work could optimize pre­
treatment parameters such as the oxygen concentration and expo­
sure time to maximize butyrate yields (Wang et al., 2024). 
Understanding key butyrate-producing microbial pathways, such as 
those of Clostridium, could aid in this understanding.
2. Microbes such as Clostridium, which dominate anaerobic conditions, 
could be isolated to study their butyric acid fermentation pathways

4. Butyric acid has applications as a biofuel or chemical building block. 
Its derivatives, such as ethyl butyrate or butyl butyrate, can be pro­

5. Controlled and efficient biomanufacturing of butyric acid and its 
derivatives can be achieved through synthetic microbial platforms 
that have been engineered with butyric acid pathways. This could 
realize the full potential of this process at an industrial scale.
6. The efficiency of waste valorization processes can be significantly 
increased in industrial settings by integrating oxygen pretreatment. 
Industries can customize VFAs profiles to fulfill individual needs for 
biochemical and biofuel production by optimizing the dynamics of 
the microbial community. Furthermore, by transforming FW into 
high-value goods, increased VFAs yields offer biorefineries impor­
tant feedstocks, supporting the circular economy.
These findings provide a foundation for regulating anaerobic diges­
tion at the microbiological level to achieve specific VFAs compositions, 
opening new avenues for maximizing biofuel and biochemical produc­
tion through efficient waste-to-resource conversion methods. The po­
tential for tailored VFAs production highlighted in this research has 
significant implications for various bioeconomic applications.
